JUDGMENT

The accused has been put up for trial for the offence under sections 302 and 309 of IPC with the allegations that he had committed the murder of his wife by strangulating and smothering her and thereafter, he also tried to commit suicide by slashing his wrists.
BRIEF FACTS OF THE CASE 1.0

As per the prosecution story on 01.06.2018, DD No. 36B was received at PS Sangam Vihar that the husband and wife were brought at the hospital, the wife was brought dead and the husband was admitted in injured condition.
SI Vivek reached the hospital and collected the MLCs.
SI Ranglal was sent to the spot to preserve the crime scene and SDM Kalkaji was informed who recorded statement of the parents of the deceased.

On the basis of allegations levelled by the parents and on the basis of initial enquiry, it was revealed that the accused Umesh had murdered his wife by strangulation and thereafter, tried to commit suicide.
FIR was registered and the matter was investigated.

After completion of the investigation, the chargesheet was filed in the Court against the accused and his other family members for the offences u/s 302, 498A, 304B Sarda vs . State Of Maharashtra, Air 1984 Sc 1622.

4.1 The accused took a defence that the deceased had an extra marital affair with one Nitin and that she was already pregnant at the time of her marriage with the accused, but was forgiven by the accused and they lived peacefully and happily.

The accused claimed that on 01.06.2018, the deceased asked the accused for permission to visit her brother in law's (jija) house but the accused forbade her as her ex-lover Nitin was also residing in the same house.
As a result of this, a quarrel ensued between the couple.
The accused claimed that he got infuriated and in the heat of the moment he slapped and pushed her.
Thereafter, out of anger, the accused tried to commit suicide by slashing his wrists.
The accused took a defence that he fell unconscious and was unaware as to what happened to his wife thereafter.
He claimed ignorance about the manner of death of his wife.
The accused however, did not lead any evidence in support of his defence.
ARGUMENTS 5.0
In brief, Ld. Addl. PP argued that the prosecution has been able to establish a water tight case against the accused.

It was argued that even though the evidence against the accused is circumstantial, however, the chain of circumstances has been duly proved and the guilt of the accused stands established beyond reasonable standards of doubt.

It was argued that from the evidence brought on record, it stands proved that the accused was present with the deceased at the time of the incident and that he had the motive as well as the opportunity to kill the deceased and that the circumstances surrounding the death of the victim prove that it was the accused and accused alone who had killed his wife and had thereafter, slashed his own wrists in an attempt to end his own life.
Counsel for the accused on the other hand argued that the prosecution has miserably failed to prove the charges against the accused.
It was argued that the story of the prosecution suffers from various lacunas and that no evidence could be brought on record to show that who had killed the victim.
It was further argued that there are no independent witnesses to the incident and that even the neighbours of the accused were not examined.
It was also argued that no toxicology report was filed and that the postmortem report also does not mention about any injury marks on the body of the deceased.
Ld. Counsel also argued that the prosecution failed to produce any photographs of the crime scene which could throw light upon the circumstances surrounding the death of the deceased.

It was further argued that the parents of the deceased admitted that no complaint to police or any other authority was ever made regarding harassment or torture of the deceased at the hands of the accused which falsifies the claim of the prosecution that she was regularly harassed and beaten up by the accused.
Ld. Counsel further argued that the prosecution has failed to prove every link of the chain of circumstances and the benefit of the same must be extended to the accused.

In support of his arguments, Ld. Counsel relied upon Sharad Birdhi Chand Sarda Vs. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1984 SC 1622.

APPRECIATION OF EVIDENCE & REASONING 7.0

In Sharad Birdhi Chand Sagar (supra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court, while examining the nature and character of proof of circumstantial evidence, reiterated its decision rendered in the case of Hanumant Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh Sarda vs . State Of Maharashtra, Air 1984 Sc 1622.

entities.text: Hanumant Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh Sarda vs . State Of Maharashtra, Air 1984 Sc 1622
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
on 20 July, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/165372234/
5 (1953) SCR 1091 wherein the Hon'ble Court had propounded five golden principles regarding circumstantial evidence.
The same are reproduced hereinunder:
"1. The circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be fully established.
2. The facts so established should be consistent with the hypothesis of guilt of the accused, that is to say, they should not be explainable on any other hypothesis except that the accused is guilty.
3. The circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency.
4. They should exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved.

5. There must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused and must show that in all human probability the act must have been done by the accused.

These five golden principles constitute the panchsheel of the proof of a case based on circumstantial evidence and in the absence of a corpus deliciti."
7.1

The Hon'ble Sarkaria J. , in Ramanand & Ors., Vs. State of Himachal Pradesh, 1981 AIR 738 while enunciating the law relating to circumstantial evidence famously remarked that "perfect proof is seldom to be had in this imperfect world and absolute certainty is a myth".

sentences.text: 7.2 In the instant case, it is not in dispute that at or around the time of the incident, the accused and his deceased wife were present in their room alongwith their one year old child.
Rather, the same is borne out from the explanation given by the accused in his statement u/s 313 Cr.PC as well as in the arguments put forth by the Ld. Defence counsel.
Admittedly, an argument broke out between the husband and wife.
It is the version of the defence that the accused got angry as his wife wanted to visit her brother in law's place where she was likely to meet her ex-lover.
Out of anger, the accused slapped and pushed his wife.
The defence claims that the accused slashed his wrists in anger and does not know what transpired in the room thereafter.
7.3 As per the medical evidence, the deceased was brought dead at Batra Hospital on 01.06.2018 at about 11:50am as recorded in the MLC Ex.PW2/C.
As per the postmortem report, the cause of death was opined as "asphyxia as a result of combined effect of anterior compression of neck and smothering and due to injury no.1 & 2.
However, viscera is kept to rule out incomitant intoxication."

The injuries as mentioned in the PM report are detailed hereinunder:
"1. A reddish colour ligature mark with whitish spared area in between of length 35 cm with varied width from 2cm to 4.5 cm faintly surrounds the whole circumference of neck in lower half of the neck with 2 petechial haemorrhage present over the left side of the neck.
Mark is 5 cm above the sternal notch and 7cm below the mentum.

Tracheal lumen is congested.

2. A reddish blue contusion of size 2 x 1.5 cm placed on the inner mucosal surface of the lower lip near midline on the right side.

7.4 As per the FSL report Ex.PW15/A, no poison or other such substance was detected in the viscera examination.
The PM report and the FSL result fly in the face of the argument raised on behalf of the accused that no injuries were found on the body or that no toxicology report was filed.

Further,
the injuries reflected in the PM report give rise to an unimpeachable conclusion that the deceased had suffered a violent death and was strangulated.
8.0 The prosecution seeks to predicate its case on circumstantial evidence as there is no direct evidence available to show that it was the accused who had murdered his wife by strangulation.
One of the circumstance sought to be proved by the prosecution is based on the last seen theory as the accused was alone with his wife at or around the time of the incident.
8.1 In Arvind @ Chotu Vs. State, Crl. A.362/01, decided on 10.08.09, the Hon'ble Delhi High Court summarized the legal position with respect to the last seen theory.

entities.text: Arvind @ Chotu Vs. State, Crl. A.362/01
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant portion is extracted hereinunder:
"103.

We may summarize the legal position as under:-
(i) Last-seen is a specie of circumstantial evidence and the principles of law applicable to circumstantial evidence are fully applicable while deciding the guilt or otherwise of an accused where the last-seen theory has to be applied.
(ii) It is not necessary that in each and every case corroboration by further evidence is required.

(iii) The single circumstance of last-seen, if of a kind, where a rational mind is persuaded to reach an irresistible conclusion that either the accused should explain,
how and in what circumstances the deceased suffered death, it would be permissible to sustain a conviction on the solitary circumstance of last-seen.

(iv) Proximity of time between the deceased being last seen in the company of the accused and the death of the deceased is important and if the time gap is so small that the possibility of a third person being the offender is reasonably ruled out, on the solitary circumstance of last-seen, a conviction can be sustained.
Sarda vs . State Of Maharashtra, Air 1984 Sc 1622.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
on 20 July, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/165372234/
7

(v) Proximity of place i.e. the place where the deceased and the accused were last seen alive with the place where the dead body of the deceased was found is an important circumstance and even where the proximity of time of the deceased being last seen with the accused and the dead body being found is broken, depending upon the attendant circumstances, it would be permissible to sustain a conviction on said evidence.

(vi) Circumstances relating to the time and the place have to be kept in mind and play a very important role in evaluation of the weightage to be given to the circumstance of proximity of time and proximity of place while applying the last-seen theory.

(vii) The relationship of the accused and the deceased, the place where they were last seen together and the time when they were last seen together are also important circumstances to be kept in mind while applying the last seen theory.

For example,
the relationship is that of husband and wife and the place of the crime is the matrimonial house and the time the husband and wife were last seen was the early hours of the night would require said three factors to be kept in mind while applying the last-seen theory.
The above circumstances are illustrative and not exhaustive.

At the foundation of the last-seen theory, principles of probability and cause and connection, wherefrom a reasonable and a logical mind would unhesitatingly point the finger of guilt at the accused, whenever attracted, would make applicable the theory of last-seen evidence and standing alone would be sufficient to sustain a conviction."

8.2 In the case of Rajender Vs. State (NCT of Delhi), (2019) 10 SCC 623, it was observed as under:
"12.2.4.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Having observed so, it is crucial to note that the reasonableness of the explanation offered by the accused as to how and when he/she parted company with the deceased has a bearing on the effect of the last seen in a case.
Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 provides that the burden of proof for any fact that is especially within the knowledge of a person lies upon such person.
Thus, if a person is last seen with the deceased, he must offer an explanation as to how and when he parted company with the deceased.

In other words, he must furnish an explanation that appears to the Court to be probable and satisfactory, and if he fails to offer such an explanation on the basis of facts within his special knowledge, the burden cast upon him under Section 106 is not discharged.

Particularly in cases resting on circumstantial evidence, if the accused fails to offer a reasonable explanation in discharge of the burden placed on him, such failure by itself can provide an additional link in the chain of circumstances proved against him.
This, however, does not mean that Section 106 shifts the burden of proof of a criminal trial on the accused.
Such burden always rests on the prosecution.

Sarda vs . State Of Maharashtra, Air 1984 Sc 1622. on 20 July, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/165372234/
8 Section 106 only lays down the rule that when the accused does not throw any light upon facts which are specially within his/her knowledge and which cannot support any theory or hypothesis compatible with his innocence, the Court can consider his failure to adduce an explanation as an additional link which completes the chain of incriminating circumstances."

8.3 Recently, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Ramgopal Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh, SLP (Crl.) 9221/2018 decided on 17.02.2023 observed as under:
"9.

entities.text: Ramgopal Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh, SLP (Crl.) 9221/2018
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In view of the afore-stated legal position, it is discernible that though the last seen theory as propounded by the prosecution in a case based on circumstantial evidence may be a weak kind of evidence by itself to base conviction solely on such theory, when the said theory is proved coupled with other circumstances such as the time when the deceased was last seen with the accused, and the recovery of the corpse being in very close proximity of time, the accused does owe an explanation under Section 106 of the Evidence Act with regard to the circumstances under which death might have taken place.

If the accused offers no explanation or furnishes a wrong explanation,
absconds, motive is established and some other corroborative evidence in the form of recovery of weapon etc. forming a chain of circumstances is established, the conviction could be based on such evidence."
8.4 Coming to the facts of the present case, admittedly, accused was present in his room with his wife and their one year old child.
The same also stands corroborated from the testimony of PW5 Kajal.
PW5 is the niece of the accused and she resided in the same house.
She deposed that at the time of the incident, she was washing clothes on the terrace.
At about 10am, she came downstairs and heard the cries of the baby girl of the accused.
She called the accused and the deceased but no response came from their room.
She informed her mother who was also present on the terrace at that time.
Her mother came downstairs and knocked on the door of the accused's room but again there was no response.
So, she pushed open the door and thereafter, raised an alarm.
PW5, did not say anything about what she saw in the room of the accused after the door was pushed open by her mother, but she simply stated that her mother raised an alarm.

The witness stated that thereafter,
she called her grandparents and that it was her mother and her grandfather who took the accused and the deceased to the hospital.
The testimony of PW5 coupled with the defence being set up on behalf of the accused as well as the explanation given by the accused in his statement u/s 313 Cr.PC,
make it abundantly clear that it was only the accused and his wife who were present in their room with their one year old child.

8.5 During her cross examination, PW5 stated that there were 02 rooms on the ground floor in addition to a kitchen and a washroom, out of which one room was occupied by the accused and his deceased wife.
A perusal of the site plan Ex.PW9/A would also corroborate the same.
Two rooms are depicted on the ground floor in the site plan.
Further, there is only one entry and exit to the house.
The room of the accused is situated on the left side of the passage from the main door.
PW16 SI Vivek Singh who had visited the spot and got the same inspected by the crime team also deposed that he had found blood on the floor of the room.
The crime team had recovered blood stained knife and a blood stained chunni from that room.
A foot mat with blood stains was also recovered from Sarda vs . State Of Maharashtra, Air 1984 Sc 1622.

the same room.
As per the FSL, report Ex.PW16/A, the blood on the articles as well as on the floor was found to be that of the accused.
The same confirms the fact that the incident had taken place in the same room.
8.6 Once the theory of last seen together was established by the prosecution, it was obligatory upon the accused to offer a reasonable explanation on the basis of facts within his special knowledge.

It is true that the burden to prove the guilt of the accused is always on the prosecution, however, in view of Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act, when any act is within the knowledge of any person, the burden of proving that fact is upon him.

Section 106 does not relieve the prosecution of its duty to prove the guilt of the accused, nonetheless it is settled legal position that if the accused does not throw any light upon the facts which are proved to be within his special knowledge, such failure on the part of the accused may be used against the accused as an additional link in the chain of circumstances required to be proved against him.
8.7 The accused simply claimed that he had himself slit his wrists and had become unconscious, so he does not know what happened to his wife in that room.
However, this explanation does not inspire confidence.
A perusal of the MLC of accused Ex.PW2/A would reveal that he was conscious and well oriented when he was brought to the hospital.
The defence of the accused is that he had slapped and pushed his wife and thereafter, slashed his wrists.
If this is to be believed, then it implies that his wife was well and alive at that time.
The accused was taken to the hospital not long after the incident.
He remained in his room till PW5 had called her mother and got the room opened.
However, it is a fact that the wife of the accused was murdered by that time.
The fact that he was conscious and well oriented belies the claim of the accused that he could not tell how his wife was murdered in the same closed room at the very same time.
This leads to an irresistible conclusion that the accused knew very well how his wife who was lying so close to him inside that closed room got murdered.
8.8 Neither PW5 nor anybody else had seen anyone enter or leave the room or the house during the relevant period.
The accused was the only one who was present with his deceased wife in addition to their one year old child in that closed room.
The door of the room was pushed open by the mother of PW5.
The deceased was found dead in that room and the accused was found with his wrists slashed.
Blood was found splattered on the floor of the room and blood stained articles including the knife used by the accused to slash his wrist was also recovered from the same room.
The site plan also shows that there is no other entry or exit to the same.
8.9 The deceased died in that room under suspicious circumstances.
Her death was caused by strangulation and smothering.
Her husband i.e., the accused was present with her at that time in the closed room.
It is the admitted case that an altercation had taken place between the husband and wife and that shortly thereafter, the accused tried to hang himself and also slit his wrists in anger.

As per the last seen theory, it was for the accused to explain the circumstances within his special knowledge, however, he gave evasive explanation that he fell unconscious so could not tell anything.
As noted above, such claim of the accused is refuted on the basis of his MLC.
Further, there is nothing on record to even remotely suggest the presence of someone else at the scene of crime who could have murdered the deceased.

10 8.10

The mother of the deceased while deposing as PW3 stated that for the initial few years after marriage, her deceased daughter and the accused lived peacefully, however, after a few years, when the husband -wife shifted to the house of his parents, the accused started quarreling with his wife and would also beat her under the influence of alcohol.
She further deposed that two months prior to the incident, the accused had tried to strangulate her daughter.
On receiving the information, she visited the matrimonial house of her daughter, where the accused had apologized to her and assured her that he would not do such an act in future.
The accused himself supplied credence to the same by admitting that a fight had taken place between him and the deceased on the fateful day.

However,
the fight was not normal or part of routine wear and tear of marriage.
The seriousness and the gravity of the altercation can be gauged from the fact that the accused tried to commit suicide first by hanging and then by slashing his wrists.
If it was a routine altercation or minor friction between married couple, the accused would not have taken such an extreme step.
This shows that the relations between the husband and wife were less than cordial.
9.0 As per the defence being set up on behalf of the accused, the deceased wife had a paramour and was already pregnant when she got married to the accused.
Even though, the initial few years went by peacefully, frequent quarrels took place between them as per the testimony of PW3.
PW3 further deposed about the previous episode where the accused had tried to strangulate the wife but had later apologized to PW3.
Further, as per the case of the defence, the wife wanted to visit her brother in law's place where she was likely to meet her ex-lover.
The accused was against it and he became angry.
They fought over it and admittedly, the accused reacted violently.

The above circumstances,
show the existence of motive on the part of the accused to murder his wife.
Further, as the accused was alone with his wife and their one year old child in that closed room, he had the opportunity to commit the crime.
There is no evidence that points towards someone else entering the room and murdering the wife.
The accused was last seen at the scene of the crime by his own family members.
No plausible or justifiable explanation was forth coming on behalf of the accused.

The mere fact that the photos of the crime scene don't exist or the neighbours were not examined by the IO do not adversely affect the case of the prosecution when on the basis of evidence available on record, guilt of the accused can be established.
9.1 All the circumstances point towards only one conclusion that it was the accused who had killed his wife by strangulating and smothering her.
The act of the accused makes it pellucid that he had the requisite intention to cause death of his wife.
Hence, his act falls squarely within the meaning of firstly of Section 300 IPC.
10.0 Now coming to the allegations of the offence u/s 309 IPC, it is undisputed and admitted case of the accused that he had on his own, slit his wrists.
Blood stained knife was recovered from the spot and sent to FSL with the blood sample of the accused.
The FSL report came positive for presence of the blood of the accused on the knife.
This shows that the accused had infact used that knife to slash his wrists.
As per the MLC, the accused had not just slashed his wrists but had also attempted to kill himself by hanging.
The injuries reflected in the MLC show ligature mark around the neck of the accused in addition to laceration on both the wrists.
The injuries suffered by the accused were not superficial but were found to be grievous.
The accused had caused such injuries with an intent to end his own life.
Nothing to the contrary could be suggested.

In the end, it can be safely concluded that the accused Umesh had killed his wife by strangulating and smothering her and thereby committed the offence punishable u/s 302 IPC.
Further, he slashed his wrists and attempted to commit suicide which is punishable u/s 309 IPC.
Accordingly, accused Umesh is convicted for the offence u/s 302, 309 IPC.
